title_ar: الكلام على صلاة المرأة في المسجد
title_en: On a Woman's Prayer in the Mosque
body_ar:
إذا كانت المرأة في بيتها تسمع الصلاة في المسجد ولا ترى المصلين بعينها، فما الأحسن لها؟ أن تصلي في بيتها أم الذهاب إلى المسجد؟

أن المرأة إذا كانت تجد مكانا في المسجد لا تخالط فيه الرجال فصلاتها في المسجد حينئذ أفضل، وإذا كانت تخالط الرجال وتخشى الفتنة أو تخشى منها فصلاتها في بيتها أفضل، ولهذا نجمع بين النصوص الواردة عن النبي (ص) كحديث أم حميد الساعدية أن النبي (ص) بين أن صلاتها في بيتها أفضل من صلاتها في مسجد قومها، وصلاتها في مسجد قومها أفضل من صلاتها في مسجد الجامع، وبين النصوص التي فيها حض على صلاة الجماعة مطلقا، بما يشمل الرجال والنساء، وإذن النبي (ص) لهن بشهود الصلاة معه في المسجد، وحديث عائشة أن النساء كن يشهدن الفجر مع النبي (ص) فيرجعن متلفعات بمروطهن ما يعرفن من الغلس،

وكذلك حديث ابن عمر وأبي هريرة في صحيح البخاري وغيره أن النبي (ص) قال: «لا تمنعوا إماء الله مساجد الله» وكذلك قوله (ص): «من شهدت منكن معنا العشاء الآخرة فلا تمسن طيبا»، كل هذا أحاديث تدل على شهود النساء الجماعة في المسجد، والحديث الأول وهو حديث أم حميد الساعدية يقتضي أن بيتها أفضل لها، والجمع بين هذا الحديث والأحاديث الكثيرة أن هذا في حق من تخشى منها الفتنة أو تخشى عليها، أو التي تختلط مع الرجال في المسجد حيث لم يكن في المساجد مكان مخصص للنساء قديما، وكان النساء يصلين قديما في صفوف وراء الرجال ولهذا قال النبي (ص): «خير صفوف الرجال أولها وشرها آخرها وخير صفوف النساء آخرها وشرها أولها» فالمقصود بالصفوف إذا لم يكن بين صفوف الرجال وصفوف النساء حائل، فأول صفوف النساء هو الذي يلي الرجال فهو شرها أي أقلها أجرا، وآخرها أي أبعدها عن الرجال هو أفضلها أي أكثرها أجرا، وأول صفوف الرجال أقربها إلى الإمام أفضلها وآخرها أي أقربها إلى النساء أقلها أجرا.
body_en:
If a woman is in her house and can hear the prayer in the mosque but cannot see those praying with her own eyes, what is better for her: that she pray in her house, or that she go to the mosque?

If a woman finds a place in the mosque in which she does not mix with the men, then her prayer in the mosque is in that case better. And if she would mix with the men, and she fears trial (fitnah), or trial is feared from her, then her prayer in her house is better. By this we reconcile the texts that have come from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him — such as the hadith of Umm Humayd al-Saʿidiyyah, that the Prophet made clear that her prayer in her house is better than her prayer in the mosque of her people, and that her prayer in the mosque of her people is better than her prayer in the congregational mosque — with the texts in which there is exhortation to the congregational prayer without qualification, in a way that takes in both men and women; and with the Prophet's permission to them to attend the prayer with him in the mosque; and with the hadith of ʿA'isha, that the women used to attend the dawn prayer with the Prophet and would return wrapped in their cloaks, not recognised, because of the darkness before dawn.

And likewise the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar and Abu Hurayra, in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and elsewhere, that the Prophet said: 'Do not prevent the handmaids of God from the mosques of God.' And likewise his words, peace and blessings be upon him: 'Whichever of you women attends the late night prayer with us, let her not touch perfume.' All of these are hadiths indicating that women attended the congregation in the mosque. And the first hadith — the hadith of Umm Humayd al-Saʿidiyyah — requires that her house is better for her. The reconciliation between this hadith and the many hadiths is that this applies in the case of one from whom trial is feared, or for whom it is feared, or who would mix with the men in the mosque — since in earlier times there was no place set apart for women in the mosques, and the women in earlier times used to pray in rows behind the men. That is why the Prophet said: 'The best of the men's rows is the first of them and the worst of them the last; and the best of the women's rows is the last of them and the worst of them the first.' What is meant by the rows is where there is no barrier between the men's rows and the women's rows: so the first of the women's rows is the one adjoining the men, and it is the worst of them — that is, the least of them in reward; and the last of them, that is, the furthest of them from the men, is the best of them — that is, the greatest of them in reward. And the first of the men's rows, the nearest of them to the imam, is the best of them; and the last of them, that is, the nearest of them to the women, is the least of them in reward.

flags.arabic: أن المرأة إذا كانت تجد مكانا في المسجد لا تخالط فيه الرجال فصلاتها في المسجد حينئذ أفضل
flags.context: the Sheikh's own ruling, the first sentence of the answer
options: render literally: her prayer in the mosque is in that case better
render as a permission rather than a preference
render the whole answer as favouring prayer at home
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW, AND THE MOST IMPORTANT SENTENCE IN THE RECORD. The Sheikh's ruling runs contrary to the way this question is often reported: where a separate space exists, he holds that a woman's prayer IN THE MOSQUE is better (afḍal), and the preference for the house is the conditional case, applying where there would be mixing or where fitnah is feared. Everything that follows is his reconciliation of the reports in support of that. An English rendering that let the well-known hadith of Umm Humayd stand as his conclusion would reverse his answer. Nothing has been softened in either direction; given the subject, the publication decision belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

flags.arabic: وتخشى الفتنة أو تخشى منها / تخشى منها الفتنة أو تخشى عليها
flags.context: the condition under which the house is better, stated twice with the direction reversed
options: keep both directions explicit: she fears trial, or trial is feared from her
flags.note: The Sheikh is careful to state the condition in BOTH directions — that she fears fitnah for herself, and that fitnah is feared from her — and he states it twice in the record, each time with the pair. Collapsing it into a single phrase about temptation would make the condition one-sided, which in English and on this subject would read very differently from the Arabic. fitnah is not in the glossary and should be added; 'trial' has been used throughout for consistency with its use elsewhere in this slice.

flags.arabic: حديث ابن عمر وأبي هريرة في صحيح البخاري وغيره
flags.context: the Sheikh's attribution of the report about not preventing women from the mosques
options: reproduce the attribution exactly as given
flags.note: This is the only report in the record that the Sheikh documents by collection; for the hadith of Umm Humayd, the hadith of ʿA'isha, the report about perfume and the report about the rows he gives narrator or nothing at all, and no gradings. All attributions have been reproduced exactly as he gives them and none has been added or completed.

flags.arabic: خير صفوف النساء آخرها وشرها أولها … فالمقصود بالصفوف إذا لم يكن … حائل
flags.context: the Sheikh's reading of the report about the rows
options: render his conditional reading as the qualification he makes it
present the report as an unqualified ruling on the rows
flags.note: IMPORTANT. The Sheikh does not leave the report about the rows standing on its own; he explicitly restricts it to the case where there is no barrier between the men's rows and the women's, and grounds that in the historical fact that mosques had no separate women's space. That qualification is the substance of his reading and must not be dropped, because without it the report reads as a general statement about women's place in the mosque, which is not what he says it is.

Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.

The source writes the eulogy after the Prophet's name sometimes in full and sometimes as the abbreviation (ص). Both are rendered as 'peace and blessings be upon him'; the source form is preserved in body_ar.
'The handmaids of God' renders imāʾ Allāh, the report's own wording.
'The darkness before dawn' renders al-ghalas, the last darkness of night; the detail is the point of the hadith of ʿA'isha and has been kept rather than generalised.

'Reconcile' renders najmaʿu bayna, the technical operation of harmonising apparently conflicting texts; this is a usul argument and the reasoning chain has been preserved rather than compressed into its conclusion.
The Sheikh gives no ruling here on whether a separate women's space ought to be provided; he treats its presence or absence as a fact bearing on the ruling. Nothing has been added.
